I read it over the July 4th holiday. This book is the author’s reflection on important common concepts of tyranny and some suggestions about what people can do to prevent it’s development. While it really is a long essay on tyranny, it is short and readable. My only critique is that I would have liked to see a few footnotes to support some statements.

No one should assume their government is immune to it’s development. Tyranny is a cancer of a society. It seems to consistently develop when governments fail to EQUITABLY meet the needs of their population. The authoritarian personality traits are found in of many populations but their numbers are unclear. We can see they exist and are adept at getting themselves into positions of power; the question is why do they exist and how do societies protect themselves from them.

The book focuses primarily on the development of tyranny in Europe over the 20th century pointing out the common traits in the process among these nations. These traits, however, can also be found in other cultures of any time in history; perhaps it is a developmental phase of human behavior and government. The problem is that, once established, it can last a long time and these are generally not pleasant or productive years for a civilization. The trick / test is be aware it can happen or is happening and counteract it before it destroys the society and government.

The author is concerned that these traits have been developing in the United States for a number of years. We have come close before but our institutions and some leaders, while far from perfect, have helped avert tyranny from taking hold. Minorities and women in our country might rightly disagree that it has been averted at all. Until we identify and pay attention to the symptoms of tyranny, we may not be able to avoid its further development. Hopefully, we will not devolve into an autocratic form of government but we will all have to work together to avoid it. The author offers some suggestions on how to do just that.

I'd liken it to a doctor telling me, "these are the symptoms of cancer, you got the symptoms, whattaya think?". How about, "you've got cancer!!"
For the sake of brevity, the book takes the chance of being light on the historical emergences of fascism.
Now for the good:
Fascism and tyranny are not inevitable, but neither is the holding of them at bay. The book does an elegant job of laying out the symptoms of an emerging fascist state, while pointing to real actions that can be undertaken as individuals to respond. It is very obvious the author is telling us something stinks while pointing in an obvious direction. Replace the coy delivery with a more pointed message about the imminent threat, and the book would have had a greater impact. It's OK to boldly call out true things.

Review Body:
On Tyranny, written by Timothy Snyder, history professor at Yale University and expert on the rise of totalitarian and fascist states, has written a short but cogent treatise about “tyranny.” The book is much like a guide that enables the reader to recognize developments that portent tyranny or dictatorship. It provides clear warning signs taken from lessons in history, notably the rise of fascism in Europe in the 1930s. It is a very timely book as the U.S. seems to be heading in the direction of fascism, if not an outright dictatorship. These are lessons of history that need to be taken seriously.
The book is very short and concise while it lays down some ground rules and watch signs for impending tyranny. “We believe we have checks and balances, but we have rarely faced a situation like the present: when the less popular of the two parties controls every lever of power at the federal level, as well as most of the statehouses. The party that exercises such control proposes few policies that are popular with the society at large, and several that are generally unpopular—and thus must either fear democracy or weaken it.” (Page 30)
One sure sign of impending totalitarianism is when facts and truths don’t matter and when the masses can’t distinguish the difference between truth and propaganda. As observers of totalitarianism such as Victor Klemperer noticed, truth dies in four modes, all of which we have just witnessed: (1) Open hostility to verifiable reality, which takes the form of presenting inventions and lies as if they were facts. The president does this at a high rate and a fast pace. “One attempt during the 2016 campaign to track his utterances found that 78 percent of his factual claims were false.” (2) Shamanistic incantation – “the fascist style depends upon endless repetition designed to make the fictional plausible and the criminal desirable. This mode involves the transformation of individuals into stereotypes like “Lyin Ted” or “Crooked Hillary.” (3) Magical thinking, or the open embrace of contradiction. “The president’s campaign involved the promises of cutting taxes for everyone, eliminating the national debt, and increasing spending on both social policy and national defense. These promises mutually contradict.” (4) Misplaced faith – the use of self-deifying claims the president made when he said that “I alone can solve it” “Once truth had become oracular rather than factual, evidence was irrelevant.” (Page 66-69)
“The danger we now face is of a passage from the politics of inevitability to the politics of eternity, from a naïve and flawed sort of democratic republic to a confused and cynical sort of fascist oligarchy.” (Page 124) “We are no wiser that the Europeans who saw democracy yield to fascism, Nazism, or communism. Our one advantage is that we might learn from their experience.”
Can Americans prevent fascism from becoming the reality of the nation? That remains to be seen. It doesn’t look promising. Professor Snyder gives us some lessons from history that we need to relearn and apply to our present precarious situation. This book is a tool for understanding the rise of fascism and totalitarianism, how to recognize it, and hopefully impede its inevitability.

Review Body:
Wow. I didn't expect such a concise, starkly written argument.

My main complaint is that the book gets a little too "Chicken Little" at times ("the sky is falling!"), particularly when drawing comparisons between our current president and historical tyrants. Snyder wisely illuminates the path we might potentially take by referencing past oppressive regimes (with a focus on Russian and German history). This alone is enough for us to be aware of how the current administration might or might not act; I found his ever-increasing commentary on the President (as if he alone were the cause of where we are today) to be, at best, a distraction and, at worst, unnecessary asides that will surely date the book. It would have more longevity if the author had just stated his examples of historical tyranny and left it to the reader to connect the dots. As it stands now, the book reads more like 85% sociopolitical commentary, and 15% "and here's why you should be afraid of Trump." Certainly those people who would read a book called "On Tyranny" are intelligent enough to apply the included theses to our own present time (no matter when that might be) without having their hand held by the author.

The real problem with Snyder using Trump as an example is that he had barely been elected at the time the book was published, so it's all predictive behavior (some of which has come true, some not). That said, while the Trump commentary weakens the book, overall "On Tyranny" is an important book with (mostly) well-thought out arguments that, frankly, should be in every classroom and on every elected official's desk. It's an excellent and thoughtful read.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 31, 2018
Review Body:
On Tyranny is a very brief book that points out 20 tactics used by certain political figures in Europe—particularly in the 30’s and 40’s—to bring about a totalitarian government. It’s meant as a warning to the reader not to fall into the same traps or be misguided by anyone attempting the same tactics. The author, Timothy Snyder, also highlights that our current president has used some of the devices employed by those tyrants of the past.

At 126 short pages it can be read in a couple of hours or less depending upon the reader. I found the book very insightful and informative. Snyder made pertinent observations such as:

“People who assure you that you can only gain security at the price of liberty usually want to deny you both.” (p. 100)

“And now, as then, many people confused faith in a hugely flawed leader with the truth about the world we all share.” (p. 71)

“When exactly was the ‘again’ in the president’s slogan ‘Make America great again’?” (p. 123)

I found the book a real treat as well as a way of feeling accomplished. Nothing like reading a book within a day to uplift you.
